segments.voice: You know that kind of news. The kind you type into the group chat, then delete. Type to your mom, delete. There's maybe one person who'd get it without a word of backstory. Mary has news like that. An angel has just told her she'll carry a child, and that her old relative Elizabeth, long given up on, is six months pregnant. So Luke says Mary goes, with haste, into the hill country of Judea. A long trip. Now she's at Elizabeth's door. She calls out a greeting. And before she can explain one thing about the angel…
screen: `NEWS YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN.` → `ELIZABETH, SIX MONTHS ALONG.` → `MARY GOES, WITH HASTE.`

segments.voice: Something happens first. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "when Elizabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the infant leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost." The baby is John, the future John the Baptist, and Luke says he leaped for joy. Then Elizabeth cries out the words you learned on day ten: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." That's where the second line of the Hail Mary comes from. Look at who's in that doorway. Elizabeth is old; Luke says she and her husband Zachary were well along in years. Mary is young, unmarried and pregnant, with a story nobody will believe. Elizabeth doesn't ask for proof. She doesn't ask how. She blesses her. Then she asks, "whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Here's one to tell a friend. In the book of Samuel, King David asked nearly the same thing about the ark of the covenant, and the ark stayed in that house three months. Luke says Mary stayed about three months too. It's one reason the Litany of Loreto calls Mary the Ark of the Covenant. Catholics call this scene the Visitation, the second of the joyful mysteries of the rosary.

segments.voice: You've seen the post: a team captioning the trophy photo the night before the final. Bold. Maybe a jinx. Mary does something stranger. Blessed in Elizabeth's doorway, she answers with a song, and the song says God has already done things that, that day, plainly hadn't happened yet. He hath put down the mighty. He hath filled the hungry. The mighty were still on their thrones. So why sing it in the past tense?
screen: `THE WIN, POSTED EARLY.` → `MARY SINGS IT AS DONE.` → `WHY THE PAST TENSE?`

segments.voice: Start with the first line, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin the first word is Magnificat, and that's been the song's name for many centuries. To magnify is to make bigger, like a magnifying glass: not making God bigger than he is, but big enough to see. Clue one comes next. God "hath regarded the humility of his handmaid." That part really had happened, to a young woman from a town in Galilee called Nazareth. She starts from what God has already done for her. Clue two: the song is full of an older one. Line by line it echoes the prayer of Hannah in the book of Samuel, another woman given a child against the odds, who sang that the full hire themselves out for bread and the hungry are filled. Mary sings in her people's old words, about a God who has done this before. Then: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." One way to put the clues together: the past tense reads less like a forecast and more like trust. Clue three is a habit. The Church sings or says it every evening, as the high point of Evening Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, so the promise goes out again each night: the lowly are lifted.

Lean a little on the verbs: hath put down, hath exalted, hath filled. Notice what it's like to say something in the past tense that the world is still waiting for.

segments.voice: Big news lands in the group chat, and one person goes quiet. Hurt? Shock? Respect? Everyone reads the silence differently. Joseph gets the biggest news of his life: Mary, promised to him, is with child, and the child isn't his. Search all four Gospels for anything Joseph says. There's nothing. Not one line. So Catholic readers have argued for centuries about what his silence meant.
screen: `ONE PERSON GOES QUIET.` → `THE CHILD ISN'T HIS.` → `JOSEPH NEVER SAYS A WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's what Matthew does tell us, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing publicly to expose her, was minded to put her away privately." The law of his day gave him harsher options. A just man, someone who keeps God's law, chooses the gentlest. Now the two readings. The first goes back to John Chrysostom, an early bishop and preacher: Joseph thought the worst, and chose mercy anyway, sparing her shame even while he was hurt. The second runs through Bernard of Clairvaux, a medieval monk: Joseph sensed the child was holy and wanted to step back out of awe, the way Peter would later ask Jesus to depart from him, a sinful man. Then the angel comes in a dream: "Joseph, son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife, for that which is conceived in her, is of the Holy Ghost." Fear not. Afraid of disgrace, say the first readers. Afraid of holiness, say the second. Both readings live in Catholic writing, and the Church hasn't chosen between them. What nobody argues about is what came next: he woke, took Mary home, and at another dream carried his family into Egypt. Catholics honor him as patron of the whole Church, a title Pius the Ninth gave him in 1870, with feasts on March 19 and May 1. Silent, faithful, and there.
screen: `A JUST MAN CHOOSES GENTLY.` · `VIEW ONE: MERCY AFTER SUSPICION.` · `VIEW TWO: STEPPING BACK IN AWE.` · `FEAR NOT, JOSEPH.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SAYS NOTHING AND STAYS.`

25.title: No room (Luke 2:1–7)
25.hook: a census, a long walk, a full inn, and a child laid in a feeding trough

segments.voice: Joseph never said a word, and stayed. Yesterday's line: the one who says nothing and stays.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SAYS NOTHING AND STAYS.`

segments.voice: Picture the house at the holidays. Cousins on air mattresses, coats piled on a bed, an uncle asleep on the couch, a kitchen too full to turn around in. Every room is taken. Now someone arrives late, with a baby on the way. Where do they go? Luke's answer is two words that stay with people: no room. And the place the baby ends up is somewhere you'd smell before you see it.
screen: `EVERY ROOM IS TAKEN.` → `SOMEONE ARRIVES LATE.` → `NO ROOM.`

segments.voice: Luke sets it up with paperwork. Caesar Augustus orders the whole world enrolled, so Joseph goes to Bethlehem, the town of King David, with Mary, very pregnant. Then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." A manger is a feeding trough. Hay, the breath of animals, the smell of a barn: that's the first bed. Now the surprise. Luke's Greek word for inn, kataluma, is the word he uses later for the upstairs room of the Last Supper, from day two. So some scholars read it as a guest room in a family house, not a hotel, with the animals brought in at night just below. Guest room full, so the baby goes down by the troughs. And there's no innkeeper in Luke at all; the Christmas plays added him. Catholics call this the Incarnation: God becoming flesh, a real baby who needed feeding and changing, choosing the low place, the Magnificat's lowly lifted, lived out. Twelve centuries later, Francis of Assisi, from day seventeen, set up a real manger with a real ox and donkey at Greccio, so people could see how poor it was. Tradition traces the Christmas crib scene to that night.

Before you step out, let one person come to mind who has no room today: no seat, no bed, no place at anyone's table.

segments.voice: When news breaks at 3 a.m., who sees it first? Not the people asleep. The nurse on her break. The trucker at a gas station. The guy stocking shelves under the bright lights. In Luke, that's who gets the news of this birth: men outside Bethlehem, keeping the night watches over their flock. Big news usually goes to palaces first. Luke sends it to a field, and to the night shift.
screen: `NEWS AT 3 A.M.` → `NEWS USUALLY GOES TO PALACES.` → `LUKE SENDS IT TO A FIELD.`

segments.voice: Luke doesn't romanticize them. Some historians think shepherds then sat near the bottom of the social ladder; others think that's overstated. Either way, David, the great king, had been a shepherd boy from Bethlehem, so the scene holds both: the low job and the royal line. An angel appears, they're terrified, and the angel says what Mary and Joseph heard too, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Fear not; for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, that shall be to all the people." The sign isn't a crown. It's a baby lying in a manger, a detail shepherds would know on sight. Then the sky fills with angels: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." Here's one to tell a friend: if you've been to Mass on a Sunday outside Advent and Lent, you've heard that line. It opens the Gloria, so every week the people in the pews pick up the shepherds' song. The shepherds go with haste, like Mary on day twenty-two, find it all as they were told, and tell everyone. The outsiders become the messengers. And Luke adds one quiet line about Mary: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart."

27.hook: two old people who waited their whole lives hold the child and say now I can go in peace
27.tomorrow: who follows a star to meet a stranger's baby?

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: The shepherds heard first and told everyone: good news goes to the outsiders first.
screen: `GOOD NEWS GOES TO THE OUTSIDERS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Loading bars. Waiting rooms. The three dots that say someone's typing, then vanish. Waiting can feel like dead time, the part of life you'd skip if you could. Luke tells about two people who waited most of their lives for one moment. Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carry the baby to the Temple in Jerusalem with two birds, the offering the law allowed families who couldn't afford a lamb. Nobody notices one more young couple. Almost nobody.
screen: `THE THREE DOTS, THEN NOTHING.` → `FORTY DAYS OLD, AT THE TEMPLE.` → `ALMOST NOBODY NOTICES.`

segments.voice: The question is old: is waiting wasted? Luke answers with two people. Simeon is just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit has promised he won't die before he sees the Messiah. How long he waited, Luke doesn't say. That day he's moved to go to the Temple, takes the child in his arms, and prays, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." I can go now; I've seen it. He calls the child "A light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel," then warns Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul. Then Anna, a prophetess, widowed after seven years of marriage, a widow into her eighties, who never left the Temple, praying and fasting night and day. Her waiting wasn't empty. It was full. So the answer here: waiting done like that is a way of watching, and it's why these two knew a baby everyone else walked past. Simeon and Anna were Jews waiting on Israel's hope, and that waiting still runs through Jewish prayer: a creed built on the principles of Maimonides says, in effect, though he tarry, I will wait for him every day. Catholics pray Simeon's words every night at Night Prayer, called the Nunc Dimittis from its Latin. And because he called the child a light, candles are blessed on this feast, February 2: Candlemas.
screen: `IS WAITING WASTED?` · `SIMEON: NOW THOU DOST DISMISS.` · `ANNA: A WAITING FULL OF PRAYER.` · `CANDLEMAS, FEBRUARY 2.` · then, large: `WAITING IS NOT WASTED.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and sit beside something you've waited a long time for: healing, a person, a change, an answer. Don't push it away or grab at it; just sit with it, the way Anna sat in the Temple. If Simeon's words are yours, let them be the last thing before you open your eyes: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace.
Nunc Dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss: Simeon's prayer, said every night, from a man whose waiting was over.

segments.voice: That was the week of the child: a doorway, a song, a silent man, no room, the night shift, and two who waited. Yesterday's line: waiting is not wasted.
screen: `WAITING IS NOT WASTED.` → `THE WEEK OF THE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Your maps app says nine hours. Would you drive that to see a baby you'd never met, in a country that isn't yours? Matthew says strangers did more: magi from the east, following a star into Jerusalem and asking, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "Where is he that is born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east, and are come to adore him." King Herod hears it, and Matthew says he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.
screen: `NINE HOURS FOR A STRANGER'S BABY?` → `WHERE IS HE THAT IS BORN KING?` → `HEROD IS LISTENING.`

segments.voice: The star brings them to the house in Bethlehem. They kneel and open their treasures: gold, frankincense and myrrh. Now what Matthew doesn't say. He never says three; tradition counted three, likely from the gifts. He never calls them kings, and Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar are names from later tradition. They're foreigners, the first in Matthew's Gospel to worship Jesus. So the feast is the Epiphany, from the Greek for a showing: Christ shown to the whole world. One to tell a friend: an old Epiphany custom chalks the new year over the front door around the letters C, M and B, the magi's traditional initials and a Latin blessing, may Christ bless this house. Then the story turns. Joseph, the man who never speaks, dreams again: "Arise, and take the child and his mother, and fly into Egypt." They leave by night, across a border. Herod orders the killing of Bethlehem's baby boys, whom the Church remembers as the Holy Innocents. Pope Pius the Twelfth called the exiled Holy Family the model of every family forced to flee.
screen: `NOT THREE, NOT KINGS: MAGI.` · `EPIPHANY — SHOWN TO THE WORLD.` · `C + M + B OVER THE DOOR.` · `ARISE, AND FLY INTO EGYPT.` · then, large: `THE HOLY FAMILY WERE REFUGEES.`
